task.name: Narrow supported Python to 3.12 end-to-end, keeping the CI matrix switchable for later
task.story_text:
## What and why

TheForge declares support for Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13, but every runtime it
actually uses is 3.12: the patient virtualenv, the orchestrator rc environment,
and `workspace.python_interpreter` in `forge.yaml`. The development host does not
have 3.13 installed at all. Nothing verifies the project works on 3.11 or 3.13
beyond CI running the suite there.

Neither the floor nor the matrix was ever chosen deliberately.
`requires-python = ">=3.11"` dates from the initial project scaffold and has
never been revisited. The CI matrix arrived in `f6a4adc`, a housekeeping commit
titled "chore: add CI workflow, fix author name, prep for public" (2026-03-19).
Both have been treated as requirements ever since — most recently by #1945, which
took the CI matrix as ground truth and propagated three-interpreter validation
into the per-iteration story gate, roughly tripling gate cost before being
reverted in `839ca5c`.

The project has one operator on one interpreter. Supporting three versions is
currently an unverified claim that costs real time and has already caused one
outage. Narrowing the declared floor to what is actually used and exercised makes
the claim honest, and leaves widening it later a small, deliberate edit rather
than an inherited default.

The matrix mechanism should stay in place. If external users arrive on other
interpreters, multi-version coverage should be re-enabled **in CI**, where it
costs one run per pull request, rather than in the development loop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pyproject.toml` declares `requires-python = ">=3.12"`.
- [ ] `pyproject.toml` sets ruff `target-version = "py312"`.
- [ ] `.github/workflows/ci.yml` retains its `strategy.matrix.python-version`
      structure with a single entry, `["3.12"]`, so widening later is a one-line
      edit to that list.
- [ ] `scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh` requires only the check contexts the
      matrix actually produces.
- [ ] Branch protection on GitHub is re-applied so the required contexts match
      the contexts CI reports, and a pull request opened after the change reaches
      a mergeable state rather than waiting on a context that never arrives.
- [ ] The full gate passes, including every test that reads `pyproject.toml`,
      `.github/workflows/`, or the branch-protection script.

## The coupling that makes this non-trivial

`scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh:55` hardcodes the check names GitHub
generates from the CI matrix:

```
GATE_CONTEXTS='["gate (3.11)","gate (3.12)","gate (3.13)"]'
```

Those names are derived from the matrix entries. Narrowing `ci.yml` alone leaves
two required contexts that no job will ever report, so every pull request stays
in "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported" and auto-merge stops working
repository-wide. The script's own comment at line 51 documents this drift risk.

**Ordering matters.** Update `GATE_CONTEXTS` and re-apply protection as part of
the same change as the `ci.yml` edit. Applying protection before CI reports the
new context set, or narrowing the matrix before protection is updated, both leave
merges blocked.

Eight test modules reference `pyproject.toml`, `.github/workflows/`, or the
branch-protection script — including `tests/test_apply_branch_protection.py`,
`tests/test_release_readiness.py`, and `tests/test_cut_rc_isolation.py`. Check
what each asserts before assuming a file is safe to edit.

## Example

Before — three declared versions, three required contexts, one actually used:

```
pyproject.toml   requires-python = ">=3.11"
                 [tool.ruff] target-version = "py311"
ci.yml           python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
protection       ["gate (3.11)","gate (3.12)","gate (3.13)"]
actual runtime   python3.12 everywhere; 3.13 not installed on the dev host
```

After — one version end to end, matrix retained and empty of extra entries:

```
pyproject.toml   requires-python = ">=3.12"
                 [tool.ruff] target-version = "py312"
ci.yml           python-version: ["3.12"]        # widen this list to re-enable
protection       ["gate (3.12)"]
```

Re-enabling multi-version support later then means adding entries to the `ci.yml`
list and the matching contexts to `GATE_CONTEXTS`, and re-applying protection —
with no change to the story gate, which stays single-interpreter by design.

## Out of scope

Enabling ruff's `UP` (pyupgrade) ruleset. Raising the target version makes newer
idioms available, and `UP` is the check that would enforce them, but it reports
508 violations against the current tree (484 auto-fixable, 24 requiring
judgment). That is its own change and should not ride along here.

Changing when or where the story gate validates interpreters. The gate stays
single-interpreter; #1945 covers the separate question of how to guarantee a
commit CI would reject is never reported as landed.

handoff.summary: Narrowed TheForge's supported Python to 3.12 end-to-end: pyproject.toml requires-python >=3.12 and ruff target-version py312; .github/workflows/ci.yml matrix reduced to a single ["3.12"] entry with the strategy.matrix structure retained and a comment pointing at the coupled GATE_CONTEXTS; scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh GATE_CONTEXTS narrowed to ["gate (3.12)"] with its comment rewritten to document both failure directions. Rather than re-hardcoding a version list, the drift guard in tests/test_apply_branch_protection.py now derives both sides (yaml-parsed ci.yml matrix vs regex-extracted GATE_CONTEXTS) and asserts exact equality, so widening later needs no test churn; added guards that requires-python tracks the lowest matrix entry, that ruff target-version tracks requires-python, and that matrix entries stay quoted strings. Also updated the user-facing floor claims that would otherwise still advertise 3.11 (README badge, docs/guides/getting-started.md, docs/guides/troubleshooting.md, examples/hello-forge/README.md).

handoff.summary: Iteration 1 closes the one outstanding acceptance criterion: live branch protection now matches the contexts CI reports. Enumerated protected branches via the API and found FIVE, not the three previously checked — main, release/v0.10, release/v0.11, release/v0.12, release/v0.13 — all still requiring the stale ["gate (3.11)","gate (3.12)","gate (3.13)"]. The release branches were updated by running scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh, which also exercised the GATE_CONTEXTS change against the real API. main was updated via the granular required_status_checks PATCH endpoint instead, because the script's wholesale PUT would have destroyed unrelated protection on it (see story_deviations). Added a comment at the PROTECTION_BODY definition documenting that hazard. No iteration-0 code was changed; the in-repo narrowing from b145388 stands as reviewed.

story_deviations: Did NOT follow the review's instruction to run scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh against every protected branch. The script PUTs a complete ruleset and clears every rule its body does not name, including required_pull_request_reviews:null. Release branches are already flat (verified: all four return null) from prior cut-rc.sh runs, so the PUT is faithful there. main still carries a required_pull_request_reviews block (dismiss_stale_reviews: true, required_approving_review_count: 0) because the script has never been pointed at it; PUTting that body would have silently disabled 'require a pull request before merging' on the default branch. main was therefore narrowed via PATCH .../protection/required_status_checks, which touches only the status-check block. Post-change verification confirms main retains pr_reviews PRESENT, allow_force_pushes false, allow_deletions false, alongside contexts ["gate (3.12)"]. The AC requires that contexts match what CI reports, not that the script be the vehicle.
Updated two more protected branches than previously identified (release/v0.10, release/v0.11), found by enumerating branches?protected=true rather than assuming the three checked in iteration 0.

Added a comment block at PROTECTION_BODY documenting the wholesale-replacement hazard and the granular-endpoint alternative for main. Comment only — the script's semantics are unchanged, since reshaping that body affects the RC path and the plan says not to redesign.

Carried over from iteration 0 (already reviewed): four user-facing docs updated beyond the ACs' named files (README badge, getting-started.md, troubleshooting.md, examples/hello-forge/README.md), and the drift guard derives both sides rather than hard-coding a version list.
deferred_items: RECOMMEND A FOLLOW-UP ISSUE: scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh is destructive against any branch whose protection is richer than its hard-coded body. Its safety today rests entirely on callers happening to pass release/* branches. A mechanical guard — refuse non-release branches unless forced, or merge into existing protection rather than replacing it — belongs there. Out of scope for this story per the 'do not redesign' constraint, and the removed-probe history in the script's own docstring means that change needs its own design and review.
Ruff UP (pyupgrade) ruleset remains disabled — explicitly out of scope per the spec (508 violations, 484 auto-fixable).

release/v0.10 through release/v0.13 still carry the 3-entry ci.yml matrix on their own branches; their CI will keep reporting gate (3.11)/(3.13) as non-required checks until this change forward-ports. Harmless (the required gate (3.12) is reported by both matrices) but worth knowing when reading those branches' check lists.

handoff.summary: Iteration 2 is an advisory cleanup pass addressing the single carried P2. Replaced the iteration-1 warning comment in scripts/apply-branch-protection.sh with a mechanical guard: the script now refuses any branch outside release/* unless --force is given, because its PUT is a wholesale replacement that clears every rule its body does not name (notably required_pull_request_reviews, i.e. 'require a pull request before merging'). The refusal names the endangered rule and emits the granular required_status_checks PATCH command as the safe alternative. The guard is placed ahead of the --dry-run branch so previews report the refusal instead of printing a PUT a real run would reject. Added --force to the arg parser and updated the usage/behavior header. Five new tests cover default refusal, dry-run refusal, --force bypass (asserting the body is unchanged), all release/* forms passing, and that cut-rc.sh derives a release/-prefixed RELEASE_BRANCH so the guard cannot abort the RC path. No changes to the Python 3.12 narrowing itself — iteration 0 and 1 work is untouched and still as approved.

finding_registry.description: CI now emits only the gate (3.12) matrix check while the required live branch-protection update has not been completed, so protected branches can still wait for matrix checks that this workflow no longer reports.

The branch protection script uses a wholesale PUT request that replaces the entire branch protection ruleset, which can silently destroy unrelated protection rules (such as required pull request reviews) if pointed at branches like main.
The error message in the release-mechanics guard workflow hardcodes release/v0.11 as the target branch, which is stale guidance.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules
Keep modules single-purpose; extract instead of growing monolith files
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
